name: Lollipop mastopexy

lead: A lollipop (circumvertical) mastopexy is a surgical breast lift. The surgeon removes surplus skin and reshapes the breast tissue through an incision around the areola plus a vertical incision from the areola down toward the crease under the breast. The nipple-areola complex is moved to a higher position, so the breast sits higher on the chest and looks firmer and rounder.

It is usually described as suited to moderate sagging, where a lift is needed but a long horizontal scar along the breast crease can be avoided. Published information consists mostly of surgical technique descriptions and retrospective case series rather than randomized trials.

paras: The procedure is performed by a plastic surgeon under anaesthesia. The surgeon plans the new nipple position, removes skin and sometimes tissue, reshapes the breast, and closes along the lollipop-shaped incision. Support tape or a surgical bra is typically used afterwards, and the final contour is described as continuing to settle over roughly a year. It can be combined with an implant or with lipo-sculpting in some cases.

As with any surgery: bleeding, infection and anaesthesia effects. Specific risks include partial or complete loss of nipple-areola tissue, wound opening, contour irregularities, asymmetry, temporary or occasionally lasting changes in sensation, and visible scars. Smoking, diabetes, obesity and aspirin use are associated with higher rates of nipple tissue loss. Scars can complicate breast self-examination and imaging, though benign changes are usually distinguishable.

angle.text: The operation physically lifts the breast and moves the nipple to a higher position, changing the contour that is visible in clothing and bare. It is generally described as suited to moderate sagging, with scars limited to the areola and a vertical line.

lead: A lollipop mastopexy, also called a vertical or circumvertical breast lift, is a form of breast-lift surgery. It uses two incisions: one circling the areola and one running vertically from the areola to the breast fold, which together resemble a lollipop. Through them a surgeon removes excess skin, tightens the breast envelope and moves the nipple-areola complex upward.[1]

People seek the operation to restore a higher breast position and a firmer, more projected shape after changes such as pregnancy and breastfeeding, weight loss, ageing or removal of implants. The visual payoff is a higher nipple position, a reshaped lower pole and a more youthful chest contour, with a scar pattern shorter than the full anchor lift.[1]
Descriptions of the technique come mainly from surgical literature and encyclopedic summaries; the evidence base is largely retrospective case series rather than controlled trials.[1]

paras: Mastopexy is surgery that raises sagging breasts by reshaping the skin envelope, repositioning the nipple-areola complex and reshaping underlying tissue.[1] Surgeons grade sagging with the Regnault scale, which compares nipple position with the inframammary fold (the crease under the breast): grade I is mild, grade II moderate, grade III advanced, and grade IV severe.[1]

The lollipop lift combines a circumareolar incision with a vertical incision from the lower edge of the areola toward the fold. Surgeons commonly plan the vertical limb to stop short of the fold so that the scar does not extend onto the chest wall. If more skin must be removed, the vertical scar can be pleated or a short horizontal scar added at the fold, turning the lift into a circumvertical-and-horizontal variant.[1]

The full anchor (inverted-T) lift adds a horizontal scar along the breast fold and allows the greatest correction, at the cost of the most scarring. Periareolar (crescent) and circumareolar (donut or Benelli) lifts leave less scarring but move the nipple less; the article summaries note that periareolar approaches can produce a flattened or bottom-heavy shape and puckered scars.[1] The lollipop approach sits between these in the amount of lift and the scar length. The same incision pattern is also used in breast reduction.[1]

Wounds are typically closed with buried sutures and adhesive strips. Support tape is commonly removed at about 7 to 10 days, a surgical bra is advised, check-ups are typically weekly in the first weeks, and the final contour is described as taking around a year to settle.[1]

General surgical risks include bleeding, infection and anaesthesia effects. Specific risks include skin or nipple-areola necrosis, seroma, haematoma, wound dehiscence, contour irregularities near the fold and asymmetry that surgery cannot always fully correct. Altered sensation is usually temporary, with permanent numbness described as rare.[1] Smoking, diabetes, obesity and aspirin use are associated with higher rates of nipple necrosis.[1] Combined procedures such as augmentation with lift carry higher complication rates than either alone.[1]

Published data on lifts in general consist largely of retrospective series. One often-cited example, a 2007 retrospective review of 40 women (13 lifts alone, 27 with augmentation), reported no medical complications, one scar revision and universal patient satisfaction; its small, retrospective design limits what it can show.[1] A 2022 systematic review has examined how long correction of sagging lasts.[1] No randomized trials dedicated specifically to the lollipop technique are described.

timeline.event: Regnault introduces the B mastopexy technique and, later, the ptosis scale still used to grade sagging.[1]
Retrospective series of 40 women with lifts, with and without augmentation, reports no medical complications.[1]
